lines.text: Lakes and volcanoes, colonial towns, foreign adventurers and a revolution that drew in the world. This is the story of Nicaragua.
In 1524 the Spanish founded Granada on the shore of Lake Nicaragua, one of the oldest European towns on the American mainland.
The same year they founded Leon, which would long serve as the colonial capital, and as Granada's great rival.
In 1821, Central America broke from Spain, and Nicaragua began its life as an independent land.
In the 1850s an American adventurer, William Walker, seized power. Central Americans united in war to drive him out.
Ruben Dario, born in 1867, became the poet who founded modernismo and changed Spanish-language literature.
Augusto Cesar Sandino, born in 1895, would lead a rebel army against the American marines for six years.
Violeta Chamorro, born in 1929, would one day become the first elected woman head of state in the Americas.
In 1936 the Somoza family took power, ruling Nicaragua for more than forty years.
Daniel Ortega, born in 1945, would become a Sandinista leader, president in the eighties, and president again from 2007.
Two days before Christmas 1972, an earthquake struck the capital, Managua, and destroyed much of the city.
Anger at the Somozas grew into revolution, and in 1979 the Sandinistas drove them out.
Against the new government rose the Contras, rebels backed by the United States, and a long war followed.
In Washington, officials secretly sold weapons to Iran and sent the money to the Contras, against the law. The scandal shook the Reagan years.
Peace came in 1990, with Chamorro elected president. Ortega returned to power later, and in 2018 protests against him were crushed by force.
From colonial towns to revolution and back to one ruler's grip, Nicaragua's struggle goes on.
